content: Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) is a type of lipoprotein that plays a critical role in the transport of triglycerides and cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues. It is one of the five major lipoprotein classes, alongside chylomicrons, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL). Historically, the understanding of VLDL has evolved significantly, with early research focusing on its role in lipid metabolism and its association with cardiovascular disease. Advances in biochemistry and molecular biology have provided deeper insights into its structure, function, and clinical implications. VLDL is classified based on its density and composition. It is primarily composed of triglycerides, with smaller amounts of cholesterol, phospholipids, and apolipoproteins. The primary apolipoprotein associated with VLDL is apolipoprotein B-100 (ApoB-100), which is essential for its assembly and secretion. Biochemically, VLDL is synthesized in the liver and undergoes a series of modifications in the bloodstream. It is initially secreted as a nascent particle, which is then acted upon by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) to release free fatty acids for energy use or storage. This process converts VLDL into IDL and eventually LDL, which is more cholesterol-rich. Physiologically, VLDL serves as a key transporter of endogenous triglycerides. It plays a vital role in energy homeostasis, particularly during fasting states, by delivering triglycerides to adipose tissue and muscle. Dysregulation of VLDL metabolism can lead to lipid abnormalities and contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. In clinical settings, elevated VLDL levels are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. High VLDL levels are often observed in conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and familial combined hyperlipidemia. The pathophysiology involves increased hepatic production of VLDL, impaired clearance, or both. Elevated VLDL can lead to complications such as pancreatitis and accelerated atherosclerosis. Conversely, low VLDL levels are less commonly discussed but may occur in conditions such as malnutrition, hyperthyroidism, or certain genetic disorders affecting lipoprotein metabolism. The clinical significance of low VLDL levels is less well understood but may reflect underlying metabolic disturbances. Treatment strategies for managing abnormal VLDL levels include lifestyle modifications, such as dietary changes and increased physical activity, as well as pharmacological interventions. Medications such as fibrates, niacin, and omega-3 fatty acids are commonly used to lower triglyceride levels and, by extension, VLDL levels. Statins may also have an indirect effect on VLDL by reducing overall hepatic lipid production. Primary prevention focuses on addressing modifiable risk factors, such as obesity and insulin resistance, to prevent the development of elevated VLDL levels. Secondary prevention aims to reduce the risk of complications in individuals with established dyslipidemia or cardiovascular disease. Landmark clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy of various therapeutic approaches in reducing cardiovascular risk associated with dyslipidemia. Future research is exploring novel therapies targeting VLDL metabolism, including inhibitors of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) and apolipoprotein C-III (ApoC-III). These investigational treatments hold promise for improving outcomes in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia or other lipid disorders.
